name: DexCom, Inc.

profile.description: DexCom designs, develops, and commercializes continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems for diabetes management and metabolic health. The company's products include the G7 prescription CGM and Stelo, the first over-the-counter CGM for non-insulin users. Q2 2026 revenue grew 13% YoY to $1.31B with 64.1% gross margin, and FY2026 guidance was raised to $5.18-5.25B. FY2025 revenue was $4.66B, up 16% YoY. Founded in 1999 and headquartered in San Diego, California.

innovation.label: STRONG
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): DexCom executed a significant market expansion with Stelo, the first FDA-cleared over-the-counter CGM for non-insulin-dependent users, launched in 2024 — opening a new $10B+ TAM in metabolic health beyond the traditional Type 1/2 insulin-dependent market [1][3]. The G7 sensor (launched 2023) delivered meaningful improvements in size, warm-up time, and accuracy over the G6. These represent one major market expansion (OTC CGM) and one successful product refresh, but not a transformative business model reinvention. AI Deployment (1/2): DexCom has integrated AI-powered meal logging (photo-based recognition on Stelo) and is developing smart basal insulin dosing recommendations using machine learning [2]. These features are shipping and differentiate the product, but are enhancements to the core CGM platform rather than standalone AI products generating separate revenue. Market Share (2/2): DexCom holds 44.7% of the U.S. CGM market and is the leader in the insulin-requiring segment, competing neck-and-neck with Abbott's FreeStyle Libre for overall market share [2][3]. The company is expanding internationally with 19% reported revenue growth outside the U.S. in Q2 2026 [1]. Product Pipeline (1/2): The next-generation G8 sensor is in development with expected improvements in accuracy, size, and cost, though no specific launch date has been announced [2]. CEO Jake Leach has referenced next-gen technology but without the specificity of named products and dates. R&D Intensity (1/1): DexCom invests approximately 16% of revenue in R&D, above the medical device industry average of 7-8%, reflecting sustained commitment to sensor technology innovation [1].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): DexCom's mission to empower people to take control of their health through continuous glucose monitoring is specific, genuine, and has shaped strategic decisions for over 25 years — from serving only Type 1 diabetics to expanding into Type 2, metabolic health, and over-the-counter access with Stelo [1][2]. The launch of Stelo at a consumer-accessible price point directly reflects mission-driven market expansion rather than pure financial optimization. The mission differentiates DexCom from pure medical device companies by positioning CGM as a wellness tool. Falls short of 4 because the mission has not yet been tested through a major crisis or leadership transition beyond the recent CEO succession. Community Impact (1/2): DexCom's core product genuinely improves quality of life for millions of diabetics, and the Stelo launch democratizes metabolic health monitoring to consumers without prescriptions [1][3]. The company's OTC strategy extends CGM access beyond traditional diabetes patients, aligning product strategy with broader health empowerment. However, no evidence of specific charitable foundation or quantified community investment programs beyond the product itself. Employee Retention (0/2): Glassdoor ratings of 3.6-3.7 and 74-78% CEO approval are below-average for tech but typical for medtech manufacturing companies [2]. CEO Jake Leach was promoted internally from COO to CEO in January 2026, indicating succession planning, but no specific voluntary turnover or tenure data distinguishes DexCom from industry norms. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying by CEO Jake Leach or other executives in the last 12 months.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Growth stock on available metrics. DexCom's financial profile is exceptionally strong across most dimensions. D/E of 53.3% is well below the 70% target (score 1.0) [1]. ROE of 38.5% far exceeds the 15% target (score 1.0, 2x weight), reflecting efficient capital deployment from a high-margin medical device business. Revenue growth of 13.1% YoY exceeds the 10% target (score 1.0), with 5-year CAGR of approximately 19.3% from $1.93B (2020) to $4.66B (2025) (score 1.0, 2x weight) [1]. Profit margin of 20.1% meets the 20% target (score 1.0). Forward P/E of 27.5 is reasonable for a medical device growth company (score 0.81). Forward PEG of 2.15 reflects moderate growth-adjusted valuation (score 0.43, 2x weight) [1]. The only material weakness is the PEG ratio, which reflects slowing growth from 16% to 13% as the CGM market matures in the U.S. Daily dollar volume of $374M provides ample institutional liquidity.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): DexCom's core business is manufacturing physical medical devices — continuous glucose monitoring sensors that are inserted subcutaneously to measure interstitial glucose levels [1][2]. AI structurally cannot replace the need for physical sensors on the human body, and the business is protected by: (1) FDA regulatory barriers requiring years of clinical trials for new entrants, (2) deep manufacturing expertise in miniaturized biosensors, (3) established reimbursement relationships with insurers and PBMs, and (4) physician and patient trust built over 25 years [1]. AI actually enhances DexCom's products by enabling better pattern recognition, dosing recommendations, and predictive alerts — increasing the value of CGM data rather than replacing the hardware. The primary disruption risk comes not from AI but from non-invasive glucose monitoring technology (e.g., Apple Watch spectroscopy or Dexcom competitor technologies) that could eliminate the need for subcutaneous sensors; however, non-invasive CGM has failed to achieve clinical accuracy for decades and remains years away from viability [2]. AI Opportunity (1/1): DexCom generates AI-enhanced revenue through AI-powered meal logging (photo recognition on Stelo), machine learning-based glucose trend prediction, and smart basal insulin dosing algorithms shipping on current devices [2].

infinite_game.summary: DexCom demonstrates meaningful infinite game characteristics — a 25-year commitment to improving diabetes management that has survived technology cycles and market skepticism, culminating in the bold expansion into OTC metabolic health monitoring with Stelo. The internal CEO succession from Kevin Sayer to Jake Leach (promoted from COO) signals organizational maturity and continuity of purpose. However, DexCom has not yet faced a true existential test of its cause, and the recent leadership transition introduces uncertainty about whether the infinite mindset will persist under new direction.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): DexCom has maintained a genuine and consistent purpose over 25 years — empowering people to take control of their glucose health through continuous monitoring technology [1][2]. This cause has guided strategic decisions including the expansion from insulin-dependent patients to the OTC market with Stelo, choosing to serve a broader population over protecting prescription CGM margins. The cause is resilient (it transcends any single product), service-oriented (it genuinely improves patient outcomes), and has differentiated DexCom from pure medical device companies. However, it has not been tested through a major crisis or validated across leadership transitions — the CEO succession is less than a year old.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): The internal CEO succession from Kevin Sayer to Jake Leach, who served as COO and was groomed for the role, demonstrates organizational stability and institutional knowledge transfer [2]. With 11,000 employees and a 25-year history, DexCom has built a stable organization. However, Glassdoor scores of 3.6-3.7 with noted inconsistencies in frontline management and communication gaps across teams suggest room for improvement in Sinek's Circle of Safety [2]. No specific turnover data distinguishes DexCom from medtech industry norms.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (1/1): DexCom operates in a competitive CGM market against Abbott's FreeStyle Libre, and management consistently frames the rivalry as motivation to improve — developing smaller, more accurate sensors and expanding into OTC to match Abbott's consumer-accessible positioning [2]. CEO Jake Leach has acknowledged Abbott's strengths in manufacturing scale and pricing while focusing on differentiating through accuracy, ecosystem integration, and AI-powered insights. The competitive dynamic has demonstrably improved DexCom's products rather than devolving into zero-sum market share warfare.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): DexCom's expansion from prescription-only CGM for insulin-dependent patients to over-the-counter metabolic health monitoring with Stelo represents a meaningful evolution of the business model — changing who the customer is (from diabetics to health-conscious consumers) and how the product is distributed (from pharmacies to direct-to-consumer) [1][2]. While this is a significant market expansion driven by the company's health empowerment cause, it is not a fundamental business model reinvention — DexCom still makes and sells glucose sensors.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): The launch of Stelo as an OTC CGM at a consumer price point represented a courageous decision that could cannibalize higher-margin prescription CGM sales in exchange for dramatically expanding the addressable market [1]. The company invested through the 2024 stock price correction (from $170 to $70) without cutting R&D or abandoning the Stelo expansion strategy. However, DexCom has not demonstrated the pattern of repeated costly long-term bets that would earn full marks — there is one major courageous decision (Stelo) rather than a sustained track record across market cycles.

investment_thesis: DexCom at $86 with a $32.5B market cap is the #2 CGM maker executing a dual-growth strategy — defending its dominant position in prescription CGM for insulin-dependent patients while expanding into the massive OTC metabolic health market with Stelo [1][3]. Q2 2026 revenue grew 13% to $1.31B with gross margin expanding to 64.1% (up 400bps YoY), and management raised full-year guidance to $5.18-5.25B [1]. ROE of 38.5% and profit margin of 20.1% reflect a high-quality medical device business with strong unit economics. The Stelo launch opens a $10B+ TAM in metabolic health beyond the traditional $30B diabetes CGM market, and international revenue grew 19% in Q2 as global CGM adoption accelerates. The new CEO Jake Leach (promoted from COO) brings engineering depth and operational continuity, while AI-powered features (meal logging, dosing recommendations) add software-like value to the hardware platform [2].
thesis_continued: The bear case centers on decelerating growth and competitive pressure. Revenue growth has slowed from 16% in FY2025 to 13% in Q2 2026, with U.S. growth of just 11% suggesting domestic CGM penetration is approaching saturation in the insulin-dependent market [1]. The forward PEG of 2.15 reflects premium valuation for a decelerating growth company. Abbott's FreeStyle Libre 3 competes aggressively on price and international distribution, and Abbott holds the dominant position outside the U.S. where DexCom needs to grow [2][3]. Product quality allegations — including claims of G7 sensor inaccuracy leading to hospitalizations, sourced from Hunterbrook — create headline risk even if unproven [3]. The Stelo OTC strategy carries execution risk: consumer health devices face different distribution, marketing, and retention dynamics than prescription medical devices, and DexCom has limited consumer brand experience. Non-invasive glucose monitoring, while years away from clinical accuracy, remains a long-term existential threat to subcutaneous sensor technology.
key_catalysts: Stelo OTC CGM market expansion — the first FDA-cleared over-the-counter continuous glucose monitor opens a $10B+ metabolic health TAM beyond insulin-dependent patients, with early adoption among health-conscious consumers and potential for employer wellness program distribution [1][2]

International revenue acceleration — Q2 2026 international growth of 19% (vs. 11% U.S.) driven by expanding CGM reimbursement in Europe, Japan, and emerging markets where penetration rates are well below the U.S. at approximately 30% [1]

AI-powered software differentiation — meal logging, glucose trend prediction, and smart dosing algorithms transform CGM from a passive sensor into an active health management platform, increasing switching costs and enabling premium pricing vs. Abbott's hardware-focused approach [2]
key_risks: Decelerating U.S. growth at 11% in Q2 2026 suggests the insulin-dependent CGM market is approaching saturation, and Stelo consumer adoption rates remain unproven — if OTC CGM fails to achieve mass-market traction, the growth narrative collapses against a 27.5x forward P/E [1]

Abbott FreeStyle Libre 3 competitive pressure on price and international distribution — Abbott's manufacturing scale advantage enables aggressive pricing that DexCom cannot match, particularly in price-sensitive international markets where DexCom needs to grow [2][3]

Product quality allegations regarding G7 sensor accuracy and a potential undisclosed coating change, sourced from Hunterbrook, create headline and regulatory risk even if ultimately unsubstantiated — FDA scrutiny of CGM accuracy standards could impose costly compliance requirements [3]
